Kandula Naga Raju, vs The State Of Telangana, on 14 August,
2024

Author: P. Sam Koshy
Bench: P.Sam Koshy, N.Tukaramji
 The Hon'Ble Sri Justice P.Sam Koshy
 And
 The Hon'Ble Sri Justice N.Tukaramji
 Criminal Appeal No.1775 of 2018
Judgment:

(per the Hon'ble Sri Justice P. SAM KOSHY) The present is an appeal under Section 374(2) of the Cr.P.C filed by the appellant - accused challenging the judgment of conviction dated 12.02.2018 in Sessions Case No.93 of 2017 passed by the Judge, Family Court-cum-Addl. Sessions Judge at Karimnagar.

entities.text: Family Court-cum-Addl. Sessions Judge at Karimnagar
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard Mrs. D.Madhavi, learned counsel for the appellant and Mr. Syed Yasar Mamoon, learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent - State.
3.

Vide the impugned judgment, the Trial Court in a case where the appellant was prosecuted for the offences under Section 498A and Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, 'IPC'),
however, found the case of the prosecution proved so far as the offence punishable under Section 302 of IPC is concerned.

Accordingly, upon convicting the appellant under Section 302 of IPC,
sentenced him to under rigorous imprisonment for life and fine of Rs.2,000/- with default stipulation.

4. The case of the prosecution, as per the charge-sheet, is that the appellant is said to have killed his wife Kandula Sujatha (hereinafter, the 'deceased') by pouring kerosene over her body and setting her ablaze.

The incident took place on 05.02.2012 at around 7:00 P.M. at Gurrampally Village,
Peddapally Mandal, Karimnagar District.

As per the prosecution, on 19.02.2012, PW.1 (Choppari Mahesh) who is the younger brother of the deceased lodged a complaint at Peddapally Police Station in district Karimnagar contending that her sister who was married to the appellant in March, 2004,
and that they had two sons from the said marriage, however, after a few years of the marriage the appellant became addicted to liquor and thereafter he used to harass his sister both mentally as also physically.
He also used to harass her doubting her fidelity.

5. It was also the case of PW.1 that the appellant used to harass the deceased demanding more and more money and on 05.02.2012 at around 7:00 P.M. the appellant is said to have picked up a Kandula Naga Raju, vs The State Of Telangana, on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/29535699/
1 quarrel with the deceased, assaulted her and finally poured kerosene upon her and set her ablaze.

sentences.text: Upon the deceased raising hues and cries, the neighbors came rushing.
PW.5 (Madireddi Ramana Reddy) who had reached the spot, poured water upon the deceased and put off the flames, covered her body with a blanket and then informed PW.1 about the incident.
Thereafter, the deceased was taken to the hospital first at the Government Hospital, Peddapally.
From there she was shifted to Government Hospital, Karimnagar and again she was further shifted to Gandhi Hospital at Hyderabad.
6. The incident is of 05.02.2012, the complaint was lodged on 09.02.2012 and the deceased ultimately succumbed to the burn injuries on 25.02.2012.

Upon receipt of the complaint on 19.02.2012, a case was registered as Cr.No.55 of 2012 under Section 498A and 307 of IPC and subsequent to the death of the deceased; offence under Section 307 was substituted by the offence under Section 302 of IPC.

The matter was subsequently investigated and the charge-sheet was filed and the matter was thereafter put to trial before the Judge, Family Court-cum-Addl. Sessions Judge at Karimnagar where the case was registered as Sessions Case No.93 of 2017.

entities.text: Family Court-cum-Addl. Sessions Judge at Karimnagar
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The prosecution in all examined as many as ten witnesses and in the course marked Exs.P1 to P10.
No witnesses were examined in defence; neither was there any document marked at the behest of the appellant.

Subsequently, after recording the statement of the appellant under Section 313 of Cr.P.C, the Trial Court finally vide the impugned judgment found the appellant not guilty of having committed the offence under Section 498A of IPC, however, found him guilty of having committed the offence under Section 302 of IPC and accordingly convicted him for the said offence and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life and fine, all of which has already discussed in paragraph No.3 of this judgment.

7. Learned counsel for the appellant at the first instance contended that the finding of guilt given by the Trial Court is erroneous as the Trial Court did not properly appreciate the evidences in its correct perspective.

It was contended that the finding of guilt is bad for the reason that there is inordinate delay on the part of the complainant in lodging the First Information Report as would be evident from the facts as it is said to be an incident that occurred on 05.02.2012 and the First Information Report has in fact been lodged only on 09.02.2012.
This itself would show that there is a huge inordinate and unexplained delay.

8. According to the learned counsel for the appellant since the complainant had reached the spot on 05.02.2012 itself would establish the fact that he was present at the house of the deceased all along,
yet he did not feel it proper to have lodged a complaint earlier.
Thus, this according to the learned counsel for the appellant is an afterthought on the part of the complainant so as to implicate the present appellant.
9. Learned counsel for the appellant tried to project the case on hand to be one where the deceased herself committed suicide and now as an afterthought is trying to falsely implicate the appellant.

That except PW.4, the prosecution has not examined another witness who is said to have reached the spot along with PW.4 and who in the charge-sheet and in the deposition has been reflected only as a neighbor.
For this reason also, the finding of the Trial Court cannot be said to be proper and is liable to be set-aside / quashed.

sentences.text: Another ground raised by the learned counsel for the appellant is that from bare perusal of the charge-sheet and the list of witnesses cited therein would reveal that there was the first dying declaration that was recorded on 05.02.2012 itself before the Magistrate, Peddapally.

Relying upon the said dying declaration before the Magistrate, the learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the said dying declaration has not been produced by the prosecution during the course of evidence and it is believed that the said dying declaration must have been in favor of the appellant and it is for this reason that the said dying declaration has been suppressed by the prosecution from being produced during the course of trial.

11. Thus, for all the aforesaid circumstances, the learned counsel for the appellant prayed for setting aside of the impugned judgment of conviction and also prayed for acquittal of the appellant from the charges leveled against him.

12. Per contra, the learned Additional Public Prosecutor opposing the appeal submitted that the present is a case where the entire case of the prosecution witnesses is based on the deposition of PW.1 and PW.4 both of whom are those who have reached the spot in the nick of the moment.

13. Learned Additional Public Prosecutor contended that from the evidence which has been collected and considering the statement of the prosecution witnesses it stands established beyond all reasonable doubts of the appellant alone to have committed the said offence and there was no other possibility by which the deceased could be said to have suffered burn injuries.

It was also contended that the dying declaration Ex.P6 clinches the case of the prosecution so far as establishing the guilt of the appellant for the reason that the said dying declaration has been recorded in the presence of a Magistrate who himself has been examined before the Trial Court as PW.7.

So far as another dying declaration having been recorded by the Magistrate at Peddapally, even though no such dying declaration is found to be part of the charge-sheet or has been adduced during the course of trial,
but the same may not have much relevance as the dying declaration brought on record is the subsequent one.
Thus, the dying declaration Ex.P6 cannot be found fault with and there is no reason for disbelieving the deceased's version in the dying declaration Ex.P6 recorded in the presence of a Magistrate.
14. Accordingly, the learned Additional Public Prosecutor prayed for dismissal of the appeal.
15. Having heard the contentions put forth on either side and on perusal of records, what needs to be appreciated at this juncture, is the evidence which has been adduced by the prosecution.

PW.1,
the younger brother of the deceased, was the person who was informed by PW.4.

When we look at the evidence of PW.1 just apposite the evidence of PW.4, it would reveal that the version of these two witnesses is almost identical and there are no contradictions, omissions or improvements in their versions.

Further, if we read the dying declaration of the deceased and match it along with the complaint lodged by PW.1 on 19.02.2012, it clearly supports the case of the prosecution so far as the incident having occurred on 05.02.2012 and the incident also having occurred at the house of the appellant.

3 16.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: PW.4 being one of the persons who had reached the spot immediately on the deceased raising hues and cries upon being set ablaze by the appellant.
PW.4 thereafter informed PW.1 about the incident and who in turn having rushed the spot and they taking the deceased to the hospital for treatment stands established.

Though there is a contention by the learned counsel for the appellant that it appears to be a case of stove burn or the deceased catching fire in the course of preparation of food, such a stand has not been taken by the appellant in defence.
Neither has he put any such suggestion to the prosecution witnesses, nor has he taken the said stand in his statement under Section 313 of Cr.P.C.
To make things worse, even the investigating agency could not gather any material with which such a theory could be contended, propounded or established.
17. Another aspect which is glaringly visible from the deposition of prosecution witnesses is the conduct of the appellant who admittedly was present at the scene of occurrence.

And if it would had been an accidental fire, the natural reaction would had been the appellant raising hues and cries, the appellant trying to pour water on the deceased, the appellant making efforts in putting off the flames.
There is no such averment, material or evidence in this regard.

On the contrary, the witnesses who had reached the spot immediately and who made efforts in putting off the flames upon the deceased have categorically said that the appellant was present in the house.

As regards the ground of delay in lodging of the First Information Report, PW.1 the lodger of the complaint himself has given an explanation for the said delay wherein he has categorically stated that since the entire family was attending to the deceased in the hospital for her burn injuries, they could not lodge the complaint immediately.

18. From the cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses particularly that of PW.1, PW.4 and other material witnesses there again does not seem to be any strong case made out on the part of the appellant in defence either in his cross-examination or by way of any evidence in defence so as to disbelieve the version of the prosecution.

19. Even though the appellant tried to project the incident to be one of suicide, but as indicated earlier, there does not seem to be any suggestion given to any of the prosecution witnesses in this regard.
Nor is there any material collected in the course of investigation or in the course of leading evidence before the Trial Court in defence.

In the absence of which, we are of the considered opinion that the Trial Court has rightly accepted the case of the prosecution to have been proved beyond reasonable doubts in respect of the incident to have occurred only upon the appellant pouring kerosene on the deceased and setting her ablaze.
20. For all the aforesaid reasons, we do not find any strong case made out by the appellant calling for an interference to the impugned judgment of conviction passed by the Trial Court.
The present appeal thus being devoid of merits, deserves to be and is accordingly dismissed.
21. As a sequel, miscellaneous applications pending if any, shall stand closed.
